title: Feed my sheep (John 21:15–25)
hook: three questions for Peter, and a closing line: the world could not hold all the books
tomorrow: To the ends of the earth

segments.voice: Yesterday, breathed: Jesus in the locked room, receive ye the Holy Ghost. Your line was peace be to you. Were your first words peaceful? Day five hundred thirty-three.

Watch the fires in the last chapters of John. The night Jesus was arrested, Peter stood warming his hands at a charcoal fire in the high priest's courtyard and said three times, I don't know him. Now it's dawn on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. The disciples have been fishing all night. And on the beach, Jesus has made breakfast, fish and bread, cooking over a charcoal fire. John uses the same word, charcoal fire, for both. Peter can hardly miss it.
screen: `A CHARCOAL FIRE, THAT NIGHT.` → `I DON'T KNOW HIM, THREE TIMES.` → `ANOTHER CHARCOAL FIRE, AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: After they've eaten, Jesus turns to Peter. Simon son of John, lovest thou me more than these? Yes, Lord, you know I love you. Feed my lambs. Again: lovest thou me? Yes, Lord. Tend my sheep. And a third time. John says Peter was grieved, because he asked the third time. Three denials, three questions. Peter answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, thou knowest all things: thou knowest that I love thee." And Jesus says: "Feed my sheep." Notice what Jesus doesn't do. He doesn't make Peter explain the denials or promise never to fail again. He asks one question, about love, and then hands him work. Each yes becomes a job. In Greek, Jesus uses two different verbs for love, and Peter answers with one of them; scholars still debate how much weight to give that. What isn't debated is the pattern: the man who failed three times is restored three times, by the same fire. Catholics see here Peter given the care of the whole flock, part of the foundation of the Pope's office as the shepherd of the Church. Then John ends his Gospel with a shrug of wonder. Jesus did many other things, he says, and if they were all written down, he supposes the world itself couldn't contain the books. That closes six weeks in John: the Word made flesh, water into wine, Nicodemus at night, the woman at the well, the bread of life, golden lampstands, the good shepherd, Lazarus, the towel, the vine, the cross, and Mary in the garden. Tomorrow, the story keeps going in a second book.
screen: `THREE QUESTIONS AT DAWN.` · `EACH YES BECOMES A JOB.` · `PETER, SHEPHERD OF THE FLOCK.` · `THE WORLD COULDN'T HOLD THE BOOKS.` · then, large: `FEED MY SHEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan to feed someone. Sit and breathe. Picture a table, or a kitchen counter, or a bag of groceries. Who in your life could use a meal today? A neighbor, a coworker eating lunch alone, someone grieving, a kid, a stranger outside the store. Let one person come clearly to mind, and decide what you'll actually give them. If you pray, you can hold Peter's answer, Lord, thou knowest that I love thee, and let the meal be how you say it. If you don't, just hold the person. The bell holds the time.
Charcoal fire. The same word John uses for Peter's denial and for the breakfast fire where Jesus restores him with three questions about love. Today's word.
Your line: each yes becomes a job. Today, turn one yes into something you actually do for someone, quietly. Day five hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics hear John 21 at Mass in the Easter season, and the Church reads Jesus's charge to Peter as part of the foundation of the papacy; feeding the hungry is one of the works of mercy.
